newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn faces more hurdles to get finances in order.
newsitem.headline: Bonn faces more hurdles to get finances in order.

text.p: The passage of three bills on Friday by the lower house of the German parliament means the bulk of the spending cuts foreseen in the government's austerity package is now through.
But the government faces further challenges ahead with its tax bill for 1997, another key element of its "Programme for More Growth and Jobs".

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's slim majority in the lower house won the day over the objections of the opposition Social Democrat-controlled upper house, but both houses need to pass the tax bill, so Kohl will need SPD cooperation.

And yet more spending cuts will be needed if the government is to meet its deficit targets, as continued economic sluggishness has held down tax revenues while boosting spending on unemployment benefits.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said no supplementary federal payment will be needed in 1997 for unemployment benefits, but Labour Minister Norbert Bluem has vowed to oppose further cuts in benefits.
The bills passed on Friday make up about one-third of the 70 billion marks in cuts from public spending foreseen in the entire package unveiled by the government in April.

Public-sector wage agreements already concluded account for a further 15 billion marks. Bonn plans to cut about 19 billion marks off its own spending, much of which will go through as the federal budget presented this week. Questions remain about how unemployment will affect spending and revenues, however.

Germany's federal states are planning to cut their spending by around 12-13 billion marks because of their own budgetary problems in addition to a similar sum they save as a result of the moderate public sector wage deal.

But The states complain that plans to cut wealth tax on operating assets next year will lead to a nine billion mark shortfall in their income. Waigel has said this will have to be made up for elsewhere in budgets.

-- Growth and Employment Promotion Bill -- 14 billion marks in savings. Raises retirement age from current 60 to 63 for men, 65 for women, effective in year 2000. Cuts pensions for retirees who leave Germany. Reduces benefits for spa visits. Decouples rises in benefits payments from salary rises.

-- Labour Law Jobs Promotion Bill: -- Relieves employers of 3.6 billion marks in costs. Cuts sick pay to 80 percent of wages. Reduces workers' protection from firing; such protection will now apply only to companies with more than 10 employees, up from five, to give employers greater flexibility to hire and fire in the hope of spurring investment.

-- Health Insurance Premiums Reduction Bill -- 7 billion marks in government savings. Cuts health insurance premiums by 0.4 percentage point, but raises patient deductible and cuts benefits for eyeglasses and dental care.
Elements of the austerity package yet to be passed include:
-- Planned delay in increase in child benefit (would save three billion marks. SPD says will block)
-- Cuts in sick pay for civil servants
-- Planned sale of real estate owned by social insurance fund.
-- Scrapping of wealth tax on operating assets.
